risk_rationale: Stagflationary pressures are intensifying: headline CPI at 3.8% and Core PCE at 3.2% remain well above the Fed's 2% target while real GDP growth has decelerated to 2.0% and NFP prints at a below-trend 115K. WTI at $109.8 and Brent at $118.3 represent a major cost-push shock that threatens to re-accelerate inflation and compress margins simultaneously, leaving the Fed with no clean policy path.
outlook_headline: Stagflationary oil shock meets a slowing labor market — the Fed is trapped and risk assets are mispriced.
outlook_body: The macro regime has shifted into late-cycle stagflation: growth is decelerating, inflation remains embedded, and commodity prices are delivering a second shock that neither rate cuts nor hikes can cleanly address. The 10Y-2Y spread at 47bp is re-steepening from inversion, historically a warning that recession risk is transitioning from fear to reality. Consumer resilience is fraying — the 3.6% savings rate offers minimal buffer against $109.8 WTI, 6.37% mortgage rates, and a credit card delinquency rate of 2.9% that is trending higher. Defensive positioning would be warranted if Core PCE remains above 3% and credit spreads stay tight relative to the deteriorating fundamental backdrop; a risk-asset rally on rate-cut speculation would be inconsistent with that data mix.

tabs.gdp: Real GDP growth of 2.0% annualized is holding above stall speed but the underlying composition is increasingly fragile against the backdrop of an oil shock and tightening consumer balance sheets. The combination of slowing NFP, a 3.6% savings rate, and WTI at $109.8 creates a credible path to sub-1% growth within two quarters. Inventory and net export dynamics could provide temporary offsets, but domestic demand is the linchpin and it is weakening.
tabs.jobs: At 115K, monthly payroll growth has fallen below the ~150K threshold needed to absorb labor force growth, signaling genuine deceleration rather than normalization. This is the weakest NFP print consistent with an unemployment rate that has already climbed to 4.3%, suggesting the labor market is a lagging confirmation of a slowdown already underway. Leading indicators in hours worked and temp employment should be monitored closely for further deterioration.
tabs.unemp: U-3 at 4.3% represents a meaningful rise from cycle lows and confirms the labor market is no longer a source of macro resilience. The U-6 underemployment rate at 8.2% — a 190bp spread over U-3 — signals significant slack in hours and involuntary part-time work that the headline number obscures. This breadth of labor market weakness is inconsistent with a soft-landing narrative and points to genuine demand destruction in the jobs market.
tabs.wages: Nominal wage growth at 3.9% YoY appears healthy in isolation but is being consumed by 3.8% CPI, leaving real wage growth near zero and providing no lift to consumer purchasing power. With WTI at $109.8, real wages are at risk of turning negative again as energy costs pass through to goods and services over coming months. The wage-price spiral risk has diminished, but so has the consumer's ability to sustain spending.
tabs.cpi: Headline CPI at 3.8% YoY is running nearly 90bp above Core CPI at 2.7%, a gap almost entirely attributable to energy — WTI at $109.8 is the dominant driver and it is not yet fully reflected in downstream prices. Core CPI at 2.7% has not broken to target and risks re-acceleration as oil costs transmit through transportation, manufacturing, and services over the next 60-90 days. The Fed cannot cut rates with headline at 3.8% and an oil shock still propagating; rate relief is not imminent.
tabs.pce: Core PCE at 3.2% — the Fed's preferred measure — remains 120bp above target and is the single most important number blocking any dovish pivot. Headline PCE at 3.5% reflects the same energy-driven wedge seen in CPI, and the savings rate at 3.6% confirms consumers are drawing down buffers rather than reducing spending voluntarily. The combination of elevated PCE, depleted savings, and surging energy costs represents a serious deterioration in the consumer's real income trajectory.
tabs.yield: The 10Y-2Y spread at 47bp has re-steepened from prior inversion, a pattern that historically accompanies the transition from recession risk pricing to recession onset — this is not a benign signal. The 10Y at 4.42% prices in an economy that can absorb current rates, but that assumption is under stress with NFP at 115K and oil-driven inflation re-accelerating. The Fed Funds rate at 3.64% leaves real rates modestly positive, keeping the Fed effectively on hold with a hawkish bias as long as Core PCE stays above 3%.
tabs.credit: IG OAS at 78bp remains historically tight and reflects a market that has not yet priced the deteriorating macro backdrop — this is a complacency risk, not a green light. HY OAS at 279bp is wider but still well below levels consistent with recession conditions (typically 500bp+), suggesting high yield is also mispriced relative to the unemployment and growth trajectory. A repricing of credit risk, particularly in energy-cost-sensitive sectors and highly leveraged consumer-facing businesses, remains the key tail risk.
tabs.housing: The 30-year mortgage at 6.37% continues to lock existing homeowners in place and suppress transaction volume, while Housing Starts at 1,502K suggest builders are still active but are running ahead of effective demand at current affordability levels. With real wages flat, savings rates thin, and no near-term prospect of meaningful mortgage rate relief, the demand side of housing remains structurally impaired. A downside break in starts and permits over coming months would be a significant recessionary signal.
tabs.oil: WTI at $109.8 and Brent at $118.3 represent an acute supply shock that functions as a regressive tax on consumers and a margin headwind for corporate America simultaneously. At these price levels, the macro transmission is unambiguously negative: energy costs are re-inflating headline CPI and PCE, compressing consumer discretionary spending, and raising input costs across manufacturing and logistics. This oil shock is the single greatest threat to a soft landing and the primary reason risk is rated HIGH.
tabs.banks: Credit card delinquency at 2.9% is a direct stress indicator for consumer lending books and is trending in the wrong direction given the 4.3% unemployment rate and near-zero real wage growth. Net interest income should remain supported by the 10Y-2Y spread at 47bp, but rising loss provisions for consumer credit will increasingly offset NII tailwinds in bank earnings. Banks with high consumer credit card and auto loan exposure face a deteriorating credit quality outlook that the current spread environment is not compensating for.

signal_flags.note: Oil at $109.8 is delivering a cost-push shock that re-accelerates headline inflation, destroys real purchasing power, and eliminates the Fed's ability to cut — this is the dominant macro risk driver.
Brent-WTI spread of $8.5 reflects global supply tightness; imported inflation via Brent pricing will compound domestic energy pass-through in coming CPI and PCE prints.
Core PCE at 3.2% is 120bp above the Fed's 2% target and blocks any dovish pivot; combined with oil shock dynamics, re-acceleration in coming months is a material risk.
Below-trend job creation at 115K is occurring while unemployment is already rising to 4.3% — this is not normalization but genuine labor demand deterioration.
U-6 at 8.2% versus U-3 at 4.3% — a 190bp gap — signals rising underemployment breadth that will compress consumer spending capacity beyond what the headline rate implies.
At 3.6%, the savings rate provides minimal buffer against simultaneous oil shock and high mortgage rates; a further decline increases the probability of a hard consumer-led slowdown.
Delinquency at 2.9% is rising in tandem with unemployment and flat real wages; continued deterioration will force higher bank provisions and tighten consumer credit availability.
Re-steepening from inversion to 47bp historically precedes recession onset rather than reflecting improving conditions — PMs should not interpret this as a bullish curve signal.
High yield spreads at 279bp are materially below recessionary norms of 500bp+; if macro deterioration accelerates, a sharp repricing of high yield credit is a high-conviction risk.
At 6.37%, mortgage rates continue to lock out first-time buyers and suppress existing home sales; combined with oil-driven inflation, housing affordability is near cycle lows.
